text:
## Observations

1. A match is an increasing tuple of positions in A, so choosing a different position for any element of B gives a distinct match.
2. Scanning from left to right and taking the first available match for each element of B gives the earliest possible position for each element. If this scan cannot finish, no match exists.
3. Scanning from right to left and taking the last available match for each element of B gives the latest possible position for each element.
4. Every match lies between the earliest and latest tuples at each position. If those tuples agree everywhere, the match is unique.
5. The two scans only need equality comparisons, and each visits at most N positions.

## Solution sketch

1. “Scanning from left to right and taking the first available match for each element of B gives the earliest possible position for each element. If this scan cannot finish, no match exists.” Scan A forward, advancing to the next element of B whenever the current values agree. Save each matched position. By induction, each greedy choice is at or before the corresponding position in any valid match, since that match’s next position is still available when the greedy search begins. If the scan ends before all M elements are matched, print `No`.

2. “Scanning from right to left and taking the last available match for each element of B gives the latest possible position for each element.” Scan A backward, starting with the last element of B and moving toward the first. The forward scan found a match, so the backward scan can finish. The same induction in reverse shows that each chosen position is at or after the corresponding position in any valid match.

3. “A match is an increasing tuple of positions in A, so choosing a different position for any element of B gives a distinct match.” Compare each backward choice with the saved forward choice for the same element of B. If any pair differs, print `Yes` because the two scans produce distinct valid tuples.

4. “Every match lies between the earliest and latest tuples at each position. If those tuples agree everywhere, the match is unique.” If the backward scan finishes without finding a difference, print `No`. This also covers M = 1, where `Yes` requires two occurrences of the target value, and M = N, where only one tuple of positions is possible.

5. “The two scans only need equality comparisons, and each visits at most N positions.” The total running time is O(N + M), including reading the input. The algorithm uses O(M) extra space beyond the input sequences because only the forward positions need to be saved.

You are a programming problem planner. Produce a natural-language guide
with exactly these headings:
## Observations
Give numbered, useful observations derived from the problem specification.

relevant observation exactly, then explain how that observation supports the step.

generation.note: Harness wall time includes Codex startup; not API latency.

usage.note: Codex token counts include its harness context; not comparable to API usage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
